clue.text: Creepy-crawly, one in which you find the Spanish caviare

indicators.note: If the Spanish is found IN something, that something has closed round it, so those two letters are planted inside the word in front.

parts.note: any small scuttling insect is a bug, and this word opens up after its first letter
one of a thing is a thing, the indefinite article
'the' in Spanish is el, as in El Greco

explanation.surface: A creepy-crawly named as the one place you will find Spanish caviare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Spanish' looks as though it belongs to the caviare, marking out a delicacy from Spain, and it is two letters instead. The beluga is a white sturgeon of the Caspian and the caviare is its roe.
explanation.definitionFit: Beluga caviare is the roe of the beluga sturgeon, and the fish's name on its own is what the trade calls the most prized grade.

clue.text: Coriander? Instead, linguistically American name that's rife online, primarily!

definitions.text: Coriander? Instead, linguistically American name that's rife online, primarily!

indicators.note: What is primarily so is so first of all, so each word of the description gives up the letter it opens on and nothing more.

parts.note: the opening letter of the herb named first
the opening letter of the word
the front letter of the adverb
the initial of the nationality
the letter this noun begins with
the front letter of the contraction
the opening letter of the adjective
the initial of the last word before the instruction

explanation.surface: An American word for coriander that people on the internet cannot stop using.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is left over to serve as a separate definition: the sentence describes the word and spells it at the same time. Coriander leaf and cilantro are one herb under two flags, which is what 'linguistically' is quietly telling you.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight the clue is what the word is: the name Americans use instead of coriander, and one that turns up constantly in online recipes.

clue.text: It's useful for Yorkshire puddings left out in the rain, perhaps

definitions.meaning: the fat that runs out of a roasting joint, saved in a bowl and spooned into the tin to make the batter rise

definitions.text: left out in the rain, perhaps
definitions.meaning: what anything is while water is still running off it in drops

explanation.surface: Somebody's Yorkshire puddings have been left standing out in the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence has no visible join and the seam falls after 'puddings'. A Yorkshire pudding is a batter baked in a tin of smoking-hot beef fat beside the Sunday roast, which is where the first sense earns its keep.
explanation.definitionFit: The fat that runs off roasting beef is kept and used to bake Yorkshire puddings, and anything wet enough to shed drops is described the same way.

clue.text: Golden Gate — first, some cake!

indicators.note: Naming the gate first sends its letters to the head of the answer, ahead of the ones the golden word hands over.

parts.note: the word itself, lifted out of the bridge's name
au is the chemical symbol for gold, from the Latin aurum

explanation.surface: San Francisco's Golden Gate, and cake to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: A famous name arrives in one piece and has to be split down the middle before either half will do anything, and the two halves then change places. The dash is there to hold the surface together.
explanation.definitionFit: A gâteau is a rich layered cake, the French word the dessert trolley uses, so it is one cake among many.

clue.text: Meaty sandwich ingredient that might be Old Norse

definitions.meaning: ox or lamb, pressed and sliced cold at the deli counter — a British sandwich filling of the old school
the language of the Vikings, one of the dead ones scholars still read

explanation.surface: A cold cut in a sandwich that may go back to the Vikings.
explanation.walkthrough: Six letters name a cut of meat and a language at once, and 'might be' is doing the work of 'for example' — the Vikings' speech is one instance, not the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold sliced ox tongue is a traditional sandwich filling, and a tongue is also a language — Old Norse being one such, which is why 'might be' hedges.

clue.text: Evidently hungry, doctor taking first slice of cake, fresh out of the oven

indicators.note: taking here means taking away, so the cake's letter is removed

parts.note: something just baked is cooling down

indicators.note: the first slice of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: first letter of cake

explanation.surface: A hungry doctor grabs a slice of cake just out of the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' is removal here, not addition: COOLING loses the C that is the 'first slice of' cake, leaving OOLING after DR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone salivating at the sight of food is plainly hungry, so drooling shows it.

clue.text: Wild misery drinking drop of Drambuie: it's only partly sweet

indicators.note: drinking means the rearranged letters take in, or swallow, the drop
wild signals that the letters of misery run riot into a new order
a drop of a word is just its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Drambuie, a Scotch whisky liqueur

explanation.surface: A miserable drinker sipping Drambuie finds it only somewhat sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: MISERY 'Wild' becomes SEMIRY, which is 'drinking' the D, a 'drop of' Drambuie, between SEMI and RY. Drambuie is a whisky liqueur.
explanation.definitionFit: Semi-dry describes a wine or drink with some residual sugar: sweet only in part.

clue.text: Appetizing cabbage stuffed with quark on a regular basis

indicators.note: A cabbage stuffed with something has it packed right inside, so the letters named go into the middle and not alongside.

parts.note: the savoy is the crinkle-leaved winter cabbage of British greengrocers, and it opens after its fourth letter

indicators.note: Taking the quark on a regular basis means taking it at regular intervals — every second letter of the word, and no others.

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the word, counted off in twos

explanation.surface: A cabbage stuffed with soft white cheese, eaten regularly.
explanation.walkthrough: Quark is a soft German curd cheese on the surface and a physicist's particle elsewhere; the clue wants neither, only its spelling. 'Regular' is the word to watch — it counts letters, it does not mean often.
explanation.definitionFit: Savoury food is tasty and salt rather than sweet, and calling a dish appetizing points at the same quality of making you want to eat it.

clue.text: Too bad! Kept a vulgar jacketed item

indicators.note: Vulgar is coarse and ill-bred, and letters behaving coarsely refuse to keep the polite order they arrived in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: Too bad — somebody has hung on to a crude item with a jacket on it.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a potato baked whole keeps its skin on and is sold as a jacket potato, the skin being the jacket; that is all the definition is doing. 'Too bad!' reads as sympathy and is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A potato baked whole is cooked in its skin, and British usage calls that skin its jacket — a jacket potato is the same thing under another name.

clue.text: Cultivated pasturage but no time for mangetout

indicators.note: Ground that has been cultivated has been turned over and broken up, and letters turned over come back in a new arrangement.

parts.note: t is the standard short form of time, and this is the letter the clue says is absent
the nine letters of the grazing land, less the T just named, leaving eight to rearrange

explanation.surface: Farmland kept in good order, with no time to spare for fancy vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: Mangetout is French for 'eat it all', the pea you swallow pod and all, and the italics mark it as the borrowed word it is. 'Cultivated' sits exactly where an adjective about pasture would go.
explanation.definitionFit: Mangetout names the flat young pea eaten pod and all, which is the vegetable British seed catalogues list under the answer's name.

clue.text: Urge nephew to get round, grand festive booze

parts.note: to egg someone on is to urge them into it
n is the family-tree short form of nephew
a round drawn on the page is a circle, the letter O
g = grand, the thousand of a boxer's purse

explanation.surface: Pressing a nephew to stand his round at Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Urge nephew to get round' reads as nagging a relative into visiting, and every word of it is a separate piece. Eggnog is the Christmas mixture of beaten egg, sugar, cream and brandy or rum.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggnog is the sweet spirituous egg drink poured at Christmas parties, so it is booze that comes out only at the festive end of the year.

clue.text: In speech, would you let Everyman drink?

indicators.note: What is in speech is heard and not read, so the words are to be written down the way they sound rather than the way they are spelt.

parts.note: asking to be allowed something is asking 'might I?', and Everyman is the setter's name for himself, so he is the I

explanation.surface: The setter asking politely whether he is allowed a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, the T slides across the gap and lands at the front of the second word, which is the whole trick. A mai tai is the rum, lime and curaçao cocktail of the tiki bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A mai tai is a rum-based cocktail, so the bare word 'drink' is a plain one-word definition of what it is.

clue.text: Adieu! Eve's off: this calls for strong drink!

indicators.note: Milk goes off when it has turned, and letters that have turned no longer sit in the order they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters; the 's is the verb 'is' and not a letter of its own

explanation.surface: Eve is leaving and saying her goodbyes, and the occasion demands something strong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eve's off' does two jobs at once: it is the departure the surface describes and the instruction to shuffle. Eau de vie is French for 'water of life', the clear fruit brandy distilled after the harvest.
explanation.definitionFit: An eau de vie is a clear fruit brandy bottled at full strength, which makes it strong drink in the plainest sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Behind boozer, fatso that's often steaming

definitions.note: The definition is a description rather than a noun: it says what is usually done to the answer, steaming being the way this pudding is cooked.

indicators.note: Putting the fatso behind the boozer sets the second word after the first, so the drinker's word leads.

parts.note: a sponge is a soak — a person who absorbs drink the way the thing in the sink absorbs water
calling a person a pudding is a British insult for someone soft, fat and slow

explanation.surface: Round the back of the pub, a fat man in a steaming temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' is the pub on the surface and the drinker underneath, and in British slang 'steaming' means drunk before it means cooked. This pudding is steamed for hours in a basin over a pan of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponge pudding is cooked by steaming it in a covered basin, so it reaches the table with the steam still coming off it.

clue.text: Flings cut short, stopped by questionable charmer

indicators.note: Traffic stopped by something has that thing planted in its path, so the questionable word goes inside rather than after.

parts.note: to shy a stone is to fling it, so flings are SHIES, with the final letter cut away
a moot point is one still open to question

explanation.surface: Brief affairs brought to an end by a man of doubtful charm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flings' looks like brief romances and is a verb instead — to shy something is to fling it. A smoothie is a plausible, over-polished man, which is the colour 'questionable' lends the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoothie is a man whose manner is suspiciously polished, which is much what calling someone a charmer implies about him.

clue.text: An apéritif or 10? No, mate, on reflection

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front, so the pieces are read from end to start

parts.note: the number 10 written as a word
taken as written
bud is American slang for a friend or mate

explanation.surface: Someone at a bar wonders whether to order an aperitif or something numbered 10, then thinks better of it.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' looks like a cross-reference to another answer, but here it is simply the number spelt out; 'on reflection' sounds like second thoughts yet reverses everything before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubonnet is a French fortified wine flavoured with quinine, drunk before a meal to sharpen the appetite.

clue.text: Reserve cash for summer treat

parts.note: reserve in the sense of a cold, distant manner — the ice in somebody's voice
lolly is old British slang for money, as in 'plenty of lolly'

explanation.surface: Setting money aside for something to enjoy in the summer.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the back half means money and the whole thing is what a child spends it on. 'Reserve' is a noun here, the coolness of a manner, not the verb the surface wants.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice lolly is frozen flavoured water on a stick, the thing British children queue at the van for the moment the weather turns.

clue.text: Greens, then fruitcake and fried pâtisserie item

parts.note: both words are slang for money, the green stuff and the stuff you knead
a fruitcake is a nut, somebody whose sanity is in doubt

explanation.surface: Vegetables, then a fruitcake, and a fried pastry to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word is food on the surface and none of it is food underneath: the greens are banknotes and the fruitcake is a madman. Frying is what sets this item apart from the rest of the counter.
explanation.definitionFit: A doughnut is fried rather than baked, which distinguishes it from the other sweet things sold beside it in a pâtisserie.

clue.text: German to wake up and complain

parts.note: g is the standard short form of German
to rouse someone is to wake them

explanation.surface: A German woken from his sleep and then grumbling about it.
explanation.walkthrough: A grouse is a moorland game bird and to grouse is to grumble; the clue wants the verb, and nothing in the surface points you there. Waking a man is what makes him grumble, which is why the sentence hangs together.
explanation.definitionFit: To grouse is to complain in a low, persistent, grumbling way — the word soldiers and workmates use for moaning about conditions.

clue.text: Woody spice — prized item — cask sent up

indicators.note: in a down answer, sending the pieces up means reading them from the bottom of the column, that is backwards

parts.note: a gem is a treasured, prized thing
a tun is a large cask for wine or beer

explanation.surface: A list of treasures: a fragrant woody spice, a valued object and a barrel shipped upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: GEM then TUN gives GEMTUN; 'sent up' reverses the whole thing, as this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutmeg is the hard, woody seed of a tropical evergreen tree, grated as a spice.

clue.text: Somewhat sombre, a stockbroker's bust

indicators.note: Somewhat means partly, so only a part of the words that follow is wanted: a run of letters inside them rather than the whole.

parts.note: the letters run on consecutively across the three words, ignoring the comma and the spaces

explanation.surface: A rather gloomy portrait bust belonging to a stockbroker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' is a sculpture in the surface and a part of the body in the definition, and a bust stockbroker — one who has gone under — is a third reading planted there to slow you down.
explanation.definitionFit: Bust and breast both name the chest, bust being the dressmaker's and the sculptor's word for the same part of the body.

clue.text: Prepare round ball that'll cleanse your palate

indicators.note: Going round something means closing about it on both sides, so the prepared word wraps the ball rather than standing beside it.

parts.note: to set the table is to prepare it, and these three letters open after the first
an orb is a ball — the jewelled one a monarch holds at a coronation

explanation.surface: A round ball being made ready to freshen the mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the job rather than naming the thing, which is why it runs on so long. 'Round' looks like a description of the ball and is the instruction that wraps one word about another.
explanation.definitionFit: A sorbet is the sharp water ice served between courses precisely to clear the taste of one dish before the next arrives.

clue.text: One particular ticket-seller vocally eschewed home cooking

indicators.note: What is said vocally is said with the voice, so the phrase is to be written down as it sounds and not as it is spelt.

parts.note: one particular seller is 'a' seller, and a tout is the man reselling tickets on the pavement outside a sold-out match at his own price

explanation.surface: A particular ticket tout announcing that he never cooked at home.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything turns on the A being said 'ay' rather than swallowed, and the T then belongs to the front of the second word instead of the end of the first. 'Eschewed' being past tense tells you the answer is too.
explanation.definitionFit: To eschew home cooking is to take your dinner elsewhere, and the answer is the ordinary phrase for eating in a restaurant instead.

clue.text: One opening function, first I reveal curry

indicators.note: Naming the function first puts its letters at the head of the answer, in front of the opening that was mentioned before it.

parts.note: tan is the trigonometrical function, tangent, as it appears on a calculator key
an opening in a wall that you walk through is a door
the pronoun as it stands, one letter

explanation.surface: An official opening the proceedings and promising to unveil a curry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' is not part of 'first I reveal': it is the instruction that moves the function to the front. A tandoor is the clay oven the dish is cooked in, fired to a heat no domestic oven reaches.
explanation.definitionFit: Tandoori names the clay-oven style of Indian cooking, and on a British curry-house menu a tandoori dish is ordered as one of the curries.

clue.text: Pupils nervously bottling beer

indicators.note: Bottling a thing puts it inside and closes it in, so the words in front are holding the letters within them.

parts.note: the letters run on without a break from the middle of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: Jittery schoolchildren putting beer into bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: A pilsner is the pale golden lager first brewed at Pilsen in Bohemia, and the name is now on half the bottles in the fridge. 'Bottling' is also British slang for losing your nerve, which is what 'nervously' supports.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilsner is the pale hoppy lager named after Pilsen, and it is what most of the world is picturing when it just says beer.

clue.text: Judge with mounds of fat, heading off for desserts

indicators.note: heading off means the word loses its first letter, its head

parts.note: bellies are rounded paunches of fat

explanation.surface: A judge with a paunch setting off for pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: BELLIES 'heading off' drops its B to leave ELLIES after J.
explanation.definitionFit: Jellies are wobbly set sweets made with gelatine, served as puddings or desserts.
